flatRate.comment: Michigan withholds 4.25% after subtracting the annual personal/dependency exemption allowance ($5,900 per exemption for 2026, up from $5,800 in 2025). The employee's MI-W4 exemption count goes in workState.certificate.allowances. NOTE: a widely-syndicated third-party page listed Michigan at 4.05% (the expired 2023 temporary rate) — the 4.25% here is from the official 2026 Form 446, not a secondary source.

supplementalComment: WIRED (a later 'go to every state' pass): bonuses/other separate payments withhold at a flat 4.25% with NO exemption adjustment (Form 446) -- reused the existing generic flatRateSupplementalFromConfig() mechanism (already built for New Mexico/New York) by renaming this field from a bare supplementalRate number to the supplementalWages.flatRate shape that helper reads, rather than writing MI-specific code. Zero new engine code needed.
exemptComment: MCL 206.30 defines MI taxable income as federal adjusted gross income (with statutory adjustments), so anything already excluded from federal AGI — Section 125 cafeteria benefits (RAB 1988-27, an actual named enumeration) and elective retirement deferrals (401k/403b/457/SIMPLE, pretax for federal purposes) — is excluded from the MI base too. This is the OPPOSITE of Pennsylvania, which taxes elective deferrals as compensation when earned. The WITHHOLDING OBLIGATION statute (MCL 206.703(2)) was fetched and read directly this session, confirming it ties Michigan withholding to the same 'compensation' concept the IRC uses for federal withholding — supporting, though not itself individually enumerating, the exclusion. 206.30 itself is still cited but not directly fetched; RAB 1988-27 remains the strongest single piece of evidence (an explicit named enumeration for cafeteria plans specifically).

source.title: MI-W4 (Rev. 12-20) — Employee's Michigan Withholding Exemption Certificate
source.verifiedBy: PDF downloaded and text-extracted directly this session

fields.personalAndDependentExemptions: Line 6 — a single count, feeds directly into flatRate.allowanceAmount x count in this engine's existing flat_rate calc.
fields.additionalWithholdingPerPay: Line 7 — a flat dollar amount added per pay period, same concept as federal W-4 Step 4(c). NOT currently modelled in the engine (state.ts's flatRate() has no field for this).
fields.newHireFlag: Line 5 — yes/no plus date of hire; feeds Michigan's new-hire reporting requirement, not the tax calc itself.
fields.driverLicenseOrStateId: Required field on the form itself (unusual — most states' withholding certificates don't require this).

exemptionClaims.$comment: Line 8 — three distinct reasons an employee can claim FULL exemption from MI withholding. All three are currently unmodelled; the engine has no equivalent to federal W4.exempt for state-level MI, and no concept of the third reason at all.
exemptionClaims.noLiabilityExpected: Standard 'I don't expect to owe MI tax this year' claim, analogous to federal W-4 exempt.
exemptionClaims.wagesExempt: Wages themselves are exempt from withholding, with a free-text explanation field on the form (no enumerated list of what qualifies).
exemptionClaims.renaissanceZone: A genuinely Michigan-specific concept NOT touched anywhere else in this dataset: certain economically-distressed areas of Michigan are designated Renaissance Zones under the Michigan Renaissance Zone Act, and residents domiciled in an active zone can be fully exempt from MI income tax (state AND applicable city tax) for the zone's duration. NOT researched further this session (which zones are currently active, expiration dates, whether it's full or partial exemption) — flagged as a real, disclosed unknown rather than silently omitted.

withholdingCertificate.knownGap: PARTIALLY RESOLVED: 'additional per-pay withholding' and the generic 'no liability expected' exemption claim are now modelled — state.ts's applyStateWithholdingExemption()/applyAdditionalStateWithholding() read certificate.exempt/certificate.additionalWithholding GENERICALLY off any state's certificate (built for Minnesota's W-4MN, but wraps every income-tax method by its shared `${code}_SIT` id prefix, so Michigan's flatRate() output is covered with zero MI-specific code — see tests/engine.test.ts, describe('Michigan'), 'certificate.exempt and certificate.additionalWithholding are GENERIC'). Still NOT modelled: the free-text 'wages exempt' reason (no enumerated categories to check against, unlike Minnesota's 6-box Section 2) and Renaissance Zone status (a distinct exemption mechanism this engine has no representation for at all).

source.title: Michigan Treasury — Withholding Reciprocity Examples (Analysis section: MCL 206.703(2), MCL 206.110, MCL 206.256, RAB 2017-13)
source.verifiedBy: fetched directly via browser; text quoted below is from the page's own Analysis section

reciprocity.rule: MCL 206.256. A resident of a reciprocal state remains subject to ONLY their home state's income tax regardless of where services are performed. This is symmetric and direction-matters: (1) a resident of IL/IN/KY/MN/OH/WI working IN Michigan is EXEMPT from Michigan withholding — the employer withholds nothing for MI; (2) a MICHIGAN RESIDENT working in one of those six states remains subject to MICHIGAN tax on those wages (the reciprocal state does not tax them, and MI does not credit/exempt them) — confirmed by the source's own Example 4 (a MI resident earning wages in Ohio Jan-Mar remains MI-taxable on that Ohio income).
reciprocity.nonReciprocalNote: Absent a reciprocity agreement, the general MCL 206.110 rule applies: MI residents are taxed by MI on ALL income regardless of work location; nonresidents are taxed by MI only on MI-source income. Example: a Tennessee resident working in Michigan (TN is not reciprocal) IS subject to MI withholding on Michigan wages.
reciprocity.mechanism: Employee claims exemption from MI withholding via Form MI-W4's reciprocity line (or an employer-created equivalent form per the source page).
reciprocity.knownGap: RESOLVED for the direction this file actually documents: state.ts's reciprocityExemptionReason() reads reciprocalStates generically and zeroes MI_SIT when input.residenceState is IL/IN/KY/MN/OH/WI, proven in tests/engine.test.ts, describe('Michigan'). The OUTBOUND direction (a Michigan resident working in one of those six states remains MI-taxable on that income per this file's own nonReciprocalNote/Example 4) is NOT modelled and structurally can't be with this engine's current architecture — stateIncomeTax() only ever computes tax for input.workState, never a separate 'residence state also wants its cut' line for a DIFFERENT state than the one being paid out of. That's a bigger, project-wide gap (worldwide/residence-based taxation isn't modelled for any state), not specific to Michigan.

sources.title: Michigan LEO/UIA — Unemployment Tax Rate (statutory formula, Section 19 of the Michigan Employment Security Act)
sources.verifiedBy: fetched directly via browser; full formula text read and transcribed below. This page independently states the taxable wage base as a flat $9,000 (no default/qualified split mentioned here), a minor inconsistency against the Taxable Wage Base FAQ page's $9,500/$9,000 split — both are Michigan's own pages; not resolved further this session, disclosed rather than silently picking one.

unemploymentInsurance.administeredBy: Michigan Unemployment Insurance Agency (UIA), part of the Dept of Labor and Economic Opportunity (LEO)

wageBase.rule: Default/statutory ceiling is $9,500. A 'qualified employer' — current on all quarterly reports, no unpaid balance of $25+ in tax/penalty/interest — gets a reduced $9,000 base. The reduction is further gated on the UIA Trust Fund balance reaching/holding $2.5B for two consecutive quarters (per the Taxable Wage Base FAQ page's own stated mechanism). A second MI primary page (Unemployment Tax Rate) states $9,000 flatly without mentioning the split — an inconsistency between Michigan's own pages, disclosed rather than resolved by guessing.
wageBase.confidence: primary_source_confirmed, with one disclosed inter-page inconsistency noted above.

rateFormula.$comment: This is Michigan's REAL structure, not a simple min/max range like Ohio's — a genuine, disclosed structural difference between the two states' UI systems. Michigan computes a rate from three components (CBC + ABC + NBC) once an employer has 5+ years of liability; new employers get a flat statutory rate for their first two years, then a phased blend.
rateFormula.constructionIndustryNote: First two years: the average construction-contractor rate (not the general 2.7%) — a distinct figure not captured here; year 3 is 1/3 CBC + 2/3 of that construction rate; year 4 is 2/3 CBC + 1/3 of it.

components.CBC: Chargeable Benefits Component = (60 months of benefits paid) / (60 months of taxable payroll), each 60-month period ending the previous June 30.
components.ABC: Account Building Component = [(Required Reserve) - (Actual Reserve)] x 0.5, divided by total payroll for the 12 months ending last June 30. Required Reserve = that same 12-month payroll x 0.0375 ('cost criterion'). Actual Reserve = all tax payments except NBC, since the business began, minus all benefit payments since the business began — can be negative.
components.NBC: Nonchargeable Benefits Component — the one component NOT based on the employer's own experience. Flat 1.0% standard for employers with 5+ years in business, reduced for employers with few/no benefit charges: 0.5% (no charges in 5yr), 0.4% (6yr), 0.3% (7yr), 0.2% (8yr), 0.1% (9yr).

rateFormula.acrossTheBoardReduction: If the UI Trust Fund holds at least 1.2% of all contributing employers' total payroll (trailing 12 months), each employer's rate is further cut by the better of: 10% off each component, or a flat 0.1% off the total rate. Does not apply to employers already at the year's minimum rate or with under 4 years of liability.

unemploymentInsurance.confidence: primary_source_confirmed — read directly from Michigan's own statutory-formula page (Section 19, Michigan Employment Security Act), not a secondary aggregator. This REPLACES the prior pending_verification 'new employer 2.7% / experienced range 0.06%-10.3%' placeholder with Michigan's actual, more precise mechanism. No simple published min/max bound exists for experienced employers the way Ohio publishes one (0.4%-10.1%) — Michigan's system is formula-computed per employer, not table-looked-up, and stating an invented min/max here would be less accurate than the real formula.
unemploymentInsurance.knownGap: stateUnemploymentEmployerTax() (src/taxes/state.ts) computes this using suiEmployer.newEmployerRate below, which is correct only for an employer's first 2 years — years 3+ require the phased CBC/ABC/NBC experience formula unemploymentInsurance.rateFormula documents in full, needing per-employer history (60-month benefit/payroll ratios, reserve balances) this engine doesn't track. employerSuppliedRateRequired is false, so a 3rd-year-plus employer who doesn't supply input.employer.stateUnemploymentRate gets the year-1/2 rate by default, which understates their real (experience-adjusted) rate more often than not. STILL OPEN: whether this state's unemployment wage base excludes the same pretax categories as its income tax withholding (the engine currently applies exemptPretax to both) — elective deferrals are commonly included in the unemployment base while excluded from income tax.

verification.regularWagesCalculation: PROVEN, not just plausible: 4 hand-derived fixtures (baseline, zero-exemption, 401k-reduces-base, section125-reduces-base) run through the actual calculatePaycheck() engine and matched to the cent — see tests/engine.test.ts describe('Michigan'). This confirms MI's flat-rate-plus-exemption structure genuinely dispatches through the engine's existing flat_rate method (built for PA), not just that the JSON looks compatible.
verification.notCoveredByThoseFixtures: Supplemental (bonus) wages, reciprocity, and SUTA are NOT exercised by any test — see knownGaps below. Only the regular-wages state-income-tax path has been proven end-to-end.

knownGaps: RESOLVED (a later 'go to every state' pass): state supplemental (bonus) 4.25% no-exemption path is wired — see supplementalWages/supplementalComment above. Reuses the existing generic flatRateSupplementalFromConfig() mechanism, zero new code.
MI-W4 additional-withholding IS modelled generically (certificate.additionalWithholding, see withholdingCertificate.knownGap). Additional-exemptions (age/blind) remain genuinely unmodelled.

RESOLVED (a later 'go to every state' pass): local city income tax (24 cities) is now computed — see michiganLocalTax() in state.ts, dispatched via certificate.residenceCity/certificate.workCity. Inter-city credit is documented but deliberately NOT applied at withholding time (it's a return-level mechanism per the data file's own text) — both cities' taxes are withheld independently when they differ.

Reciprocity's INBOUND direction (6 states) IS implemented — see reciprocity.knownGap above. The OUTBOUND direction (a MI resident working in a reciprocal state) remains a genuine, project-wide architecture gap, not MI-specific.

Employer SUTA is computed for Michigan — stateUnemploymentEmployerTax() reads the normalized suiEmployer block, using the employer's own assigned rate when the caller supplies one and the published new-employer rate otherwise. See unemploymentInsurance.knownGap for what's still open (years 3+ experience-rating requires per-employer history this engine doesn't track).

suiEmployer.$comment: Normalized employer-side unemployment parameters — the shape src/taxes/state.ts reads. The detailed unemploymentInsurance block above stays the record of research; this exists because that block's shape varies too much between states to compute from directly (wage bases as objects, industry-keyed rate maps, differently-named keys).
suiEmployer.wageBaseSource: CORRECTED 2026-09-06 (found on a 'go to every state, fix real bugs not just disclose them' pass): this had been flattened to a bare 9000 — the QUALIFIED-employer figure applied unconditionally to every employer — even though unemploymentInsurance.wageBase above had already documented the real $9,500 default / $9,000 qualified split with its own primary source. Applying $9,000 to a non-qualified employer under-caps (and so under-withholds/under-remits) their SUTA by $500 of wages. stateUnemploymentEmployerTax() in src/taxes/state.ts now reads this as a two-tier object, resolved via EmployerContext.stateUnemploymentQualifiedForReducedWageBase (keyed by state code, caller-supplied) — defaulting to the $9,500 statutory base when the caller doesn't affirmatively say the employer qualifies, since the reduced base is an opt-in discount, not something to assume in the caller's favor.
suiEmployer.newEmployerRateSource: Matches unemploymentInsurance.rateFormula.newEmployerSchedule.year1/year2 above exactly (both 0.027) — primary_source_confirmed from Michigan's own Section 19 statutory-formula page, not just the earlier OnPay secondary figure this field cites historically. Correct ONLY for an employer's first 2 years; years 3+ require the phased CBC/ABC/NBC formula unemploymentInsurance.rateFormula documents in full, which this engine has no per-employer history (60-month benefit/payroll ratios, reserve balances) to compute — same disclosed structural limit as before, unchanged by this pass.
suiEmployer.experienceRangeNote: CORRECTED 2026-09-06: this field previously stated an invented {min: 0.0006, max: 0.103} range that directly contradicted unemploymentInsurance.confidence above, which explicitly says 'No simple published min/max bound exists for experienced employers ... stating an invented min/max here would be less accurate than the real formula.' The field was never actually READ by stateUnemploymentEmployerTax() (confirmed by reading the function) so this was a self-contradictory, unused, silently-stale value, not a live calculation bug — but a real data-integrity issue worth fixing on its own, the same class of 'disclosed gap says one thing, the actual field says another' error as WV's Charleston rate and Denver's false already-wired claim elsewhere in this project.
suiEmployer.confidence: primary_source_confirmed for the wage base and the year-1/2 new-employer rate (both now consistent with unemploymentInsurance above); years 3+ genuinely unmodellable without per-employer history, disclosed rather than approximated.
